subtitle: Help your team bring questions, concerns and uncertainty into its decisions in ways that are useful. Professional standards and the right formal routes stay in place throughout.
scope: For leaders, supervisors, and team leads improving team learning and decision practices. Psychological safety is a team-learning concept, not a clinical diagnosis, a guarantee of confidentiality, or a replacement for reporting, investigation, emergency, or accountability procedures. This course does not assess individual employees or assign a validated team score. Practice cases are practice.
introTranscript: Teams need information that people may hesitate to share: a missing assumption, a mistake, a question, or a concern about a proposed decision. Psychological safety concerns whether people expect that taking such interpersonal risks will be met without humiliation or inappropriate punishment. This course uses that concept to examine a service-review team. Leaders practice inviting useful input, responding constructively, learning from errors, and checking whether concerns reach decisions. The course does not promise that every idea will be accepted or every difficult conversation comfortable. It connects thoughtful participation to clear standards, appropriate authority, and follow-through.

intro.heading: Understand what the team-learning concept does and does not mean
intro.body:
Psychological safety concerns whether people expect that asking questions, raising concerns, or admitting mistakes will lead to humiliation or inappropriate punishment. It is a shared team expectation, rather than a label describing an individual’s courage or personality. Research connects the concept with learning behavior, but a leader cannot guarantee a particular outcome simply by announcing a safe space.

In a service-review team, a staff member questions whether a proposed form excludes people using assistive technology. The question may challenge the plan without attacking anyone. The team can examine it seriously and still decide that an idea needs further evidence or cannot be implemented as suggested.

Do not promise unlimited confidentiality, no accountability, or freedom from every uncomfortable discussion. Formal reporting and response duties continue. The leader’s practical role is to make useful questions possible, respond professionally, and keep decisions connected to evidence and authority rather than ridicule or unquestioning agreement.

flashcards.back: A team-learning concept concerning people’s expectation that they can raise questions, concerns, ideas, or mistakes without humiliation or inappropriate punishment.
The possible social cost of asking for help, disagreeing, or admitting uncertainty in front of others.
A practical opportunity to contribute, with a clear question, usable route, and enough time to respond.
A response that examines the content and next step without ridiculing the contributor.
Examination of how work occurred and what should improve, separate from any required formal finding or accountability process.
Showing what happened to a contribution or concern and who is responsible for the next step.

items.title: Team expectation
items.body: The issue is what people expect will happen when they take an interpersonal risk. A staff member may have useful knowledge but hesitate because earlier questions were mocked. Examine the team’s response practices rather than blame the person for insufficient confidence or assign an individual safety rating.

items.title: Standards
items.body: Clear standards can coexist with respectful questioning. In the form-review case, staff still need a usable and accurate product by an appropriate date. Inviting a concern about access does not waive those requirements; it gives the team information needed to meet them more reliably.

items.title: Boundaries
items.body: A team-learning promise cannot override complaint, records, or emergency responsibilities. If a report alleges discrimination, the leader must use the proper route rather than keep it inside an informal safe-space discussion. Explain limits honestly and distinguish learning conversation from formal action.

tabs.label: Agreement as safety
tabs.body: A meeting with no disagreement can feel smooth, but agreement does not establish that questions were possible. People may lack information or expect a negative response. Examine how input is invited and treated instead of using consensus as proof of a healthy process.

tabs.label: Questioning with standards
tabs.body: Questioning with standards makes the purpose and evidence clear while allowing uncertainty to be raised. It helps the team examine a real decision. An idea can be declined professionally when its substance is considered and the reason is explained.

tabs.label: No consequences promise
tabs.body: A promise of no consequences may sound welcoming, but can conflict with legitimate accountability and formal duties. State that people can raise concerns professionally and explain appropriate routes. Do not promise protections or secrecy beyond the leader’s authority.

check.question: Which statement correctly frames psychological safety?
check.correct: A team should support useful questions and concerns without humiliation while retaining standards and formal duties.
wrong: No disagreement proves the team is safe.
All reports can remain secret inside the team.
check.feedbackCorrect: The framing connects speaking up to learning without removing judgment, accountability, or required processes.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Adopting every idea removes decision responsibility, and silence cannot prove that speaking up is possible. Absolute secrecy can also conflict with formal duties. Support professional questioning while keeping evidence, standards, and appropriate routes clear.

items.text: A person can raise a missing assumption without ridicule.
The team can ask for help when knowledge is incomplete.
The final form must be usable and accurate.
The proper complaint process remains available.
Every idea will be accepted.
No information will ever need another authorized office.

scenario.context: DHS practice case: The leader announces that safety means every idea is accepted and nothing said can ever leave the group.

Invite professional questions while explaining standards, authority, and formal privacy limits.
Avoid all participation because the promises were too broad.
responses: The promises exceed the concept and the leader’s authority.
This makes the learning purpose and its boundaries accurate.
Participation can continue with appropriate boundaries.

move.control: You can frame questioning and expectations honestly.
move.failure: A learning invitation becomes an impossible guarantee.

intro.heading: Invite useful input before the decision closes
intro.body:
“Any questions?” is often too broad or too late to reveal an important concern. A useful invitation identifies what the team is deciding, what remains uncertain, and how people can respond before the choice closes. People may need preparation, a written route, or a smaller conversation to contribute relevant information.

In the practice form-review team, the leader asks for concerns after the design is sent for approval. A staff member had identified an access problem but did not interrupt the fast discussion. Providing the draft earlier and asking specifically about access barriers gives the concern a better chance to reach the decision.

Do not require every person to speak publicly or explain a personal experience. Offer appropriate routes and show how input will be considered. If the decision is already fixed, say what can still be influenced. An invitation that conceals its limits risks turning participation into ceremony rather than useful learning.

Identify a participation route that excludes a relevant contribution.

What should change?
lessons.keyStatement: An invitation needs a real opportunity, not just welcoming words.

items.title: Question
items.body: Ask about a concrete uncertainty, such as what could prevent people from using the form. This gives staff a defined task and can surface information the leader lacks. A broad request for positivity or team agreement does not serve the same purpose because it discourages the very concern the decision needs.

items.title: Timing
items.body: Invite input while there is still a meaningful path to act on it. In the form-review case, a late question after submission makes correction harder. Share the material with enough appropriate preparation and identify the input deadline and decision responsibility without promising that every suggestion will be used.

items.title: Route
items.body: A written route or planned discussion can complement spoken input. The purpose is to capture relevant knowledge, not rank courage or force personal disclosure. Confirm that the route actually reaches the person reviewing the decision; an unread comment box is not a usable alternative.

tabs.label: Late broad invitation
tabs.body: A late broad invitation is easy to add to an agenda but may leave the decision effectively closed. It can make lack of response look like agreement. Identify what remains open and ask a focused question before the relevant review point.

tabs.label: Usable alternatives
tabs.body: Usable alternatives let people contribute through a route that fits the task and conditions. They require clear timing and review responsibility. A written comment route only helps when the team knows how the comments will reach the actual decision.

tabs.label: Forced disclosure
tabs.body: Forcing everyone to share a personal story can create pressure and collect information unnecessary to the decision. Invite evidence and perspectives without demanding an identity or experience narrative. People can contribute a practical concern without representing an entire group.

check.question: What makes the form-review invitation useful?
check.correct: A focused access question, timely material, and a response route that reaches the decision.
wrong: Require a personal story from each employee.
check.feedbackCorrect: The invitation gives relevant knowledge a usable path into a decision that can still respond.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Late timing, forced personal stories, and assumed approval all narrow meaningful participation. A useful invitation names the uncertainty, provides appropriate preparation, and explains how input reaches the decision without requiring disclosure.

items.text: What could prevent a person from using this form?
Which assumption in the draft needs evidence?
Written comments are reviewed before the choice closes.
The leader identifies who receives and considers input.
Questions are invited only after final submission.
Everyone must disclose a personal experience to contribute.

scenario.context: DHS practice case: The leader asks for feedback after the form is submitted and then says staff had their chance.
options: Repeat the same late question more loudly.
Invite focused input with usable preparation and response routes before the decision closes.
responses: Volume does not repair timing or influence.
This turns the invitation into a practical opportunity.
Personal disclosure is not required to identify a design issue.

lessons.transfer: Choose one decision uncertainty and plan when and how contributions will be considered.

move.control: You can design the timing, question, and route for input.
move.failure: A ceremonial invitation is mistaken for meaningful participation.

objectives: Prepare a constructive response to a question that challenges a plan.

intro.heading: Respond to a concern by examining its content
intro.body:
People learn from what happens after someone speaks. If a leader invites questions and then mocks the first one, the invitation loses meaning. A constructive response acknowledges the contribution, checks its substance, and explains what will happen next. It need not agree with every claim or accept an unsupported suggestion.

In the practice form-review meeting, a staff member asks whether a mandatory field could exclude people without the requested document. The leader says the employee is always negative. That labels the person instead of examining the question. A useful response asks what evidence is available and who can verify the requirement.

The leader can state uncertainty and seek help without surrendering the decision. When the concern needs a formal complaint or other authority route, explain and use it. Do not absorb every report into ordinary group discussion. What matters is an appropriate response to the actual content, with professional treatment and clear follow-through.

Distinguish content evaluation from a personal judgment about the contributor.

lessons.keyStatement: The response tells the team whether the invitation was real.

items.title: Acknowledge
items.body: Acknowledge the contribution without demanding that the person defend the right to raise it. In the field-requirement case, a brief thanks can reduce immediate dismissal. It must be followed by attention to the content; politeness alone does not examine whether the form has a real access problem.

items.title: Examine
items.body: Separate the question from the contributor’s presumed attitude. Ask whether the field is required, what alternatives exist, and which evidence or office can answer. If the suggestion is not feasible, explain the reason rather than describe the employee as negative or disloyal.

items.title: Next step
items.body: State who will check the issue, what can be shared, and when the team will revisit it. If the question involves a requirement outside the leader’s authority, route it properly. Saying “we will look at it” without responsibility can leave the concern parked indefinitely and make the invitation appear empty.

tabs.label: Personal label
tabs.body: Calling the contributor negative can make the discussion seem efficient, but substitutes an attitude judgment for the missing information. Others may infer that challenging the plan carries a social penalty. Return to the specific question and evidence.

tabs.label: Constructive examination
tabs.body: Constructive examination can agree, disagree, or defer pending evidence. Its value is that the contribution receives a substantive response. Clear responsibility and a next review make uncertainty usable rather than leaving the person to interpret silence.

tabs.label: Polite dismissal
tabs.body: A polite thank-you followed by no examination can look welcoming while leaving the issue untouched. Treat the acknowledgment as the beginning. Explain whether the issue will be checked, why it is outside scope, or which route applies instead.

check.question: How should the leader respond to the mandatory-field question?
check.correct: Examine the requirement and access implications, identify evidence or authority, and explain the next step.
wrong: Thank the employee and ignore the question.
Adopt the suggestion without checking the requirement.
check.feedbackCorrect: The response treats the content seriously without replacing analysis or authority with automatic agreement.
check.feedbackIncorrect: A personal label and polite dismissal both leave the substance unexamined. Automatic adoption also bypasses relevant requirements. Acknowledge the question, check the evidence and authority, and identify what happens next.

items.text: Identify who will verify the requirement.
Explain the reason if an option cannot be used.
Could a missing document block access?
What authority requires the field?
The employee is called negative for asking.
The leader invites questions and mocks the first one.

options: Defend the label to preserve confidence.
Return to the content and coordinate the evidence or authority needed to answer it.
Remove the field immediately without checking its purpose.
responses: The label still does not answer the concern.
This supports learning while retaining decision responsibility.
The requirement needs examination rather than a new shortcut.

lessons.transfer: Draft a response with acknowledgment, a substantive question, a responsible next step, and no personal label.

move.control: You can respond to the content and keep the next step visible.
move.failure: A contribution becomes a judgment about the contributor.

intro.heading: Learn from a mistake without replacing accountability
intro.body:
When someone identifies a mistake, the team can examine how the work occurred and what needs improvement. That learning does not mean every error is acceptable or that formal accountability disappears. Different concerns require different procedures. A supervisor should not use a learning meeting to make a disciplinary finding or promise that no required response will occur.

In the practice form-review team, an outdated eligibility note reaches the draft because the source owner was unclear and the final check used a stale file. The team can correct the material and clarify the source-check responsibility. Blaming one person publicly may hide the process gap; refusing to discuss relevant responsibility leaves a different gap.

Separate the factual correction, learning question, and any formal matter requiring HR, legal, or other authority. Use approved information and avoid reproducing personal complaint or participant records. A useful learning review produces a specific change and follow-up, rather than a declaration that the team should celebrate every failure or punish every mistake.

inThisLesson: Distinguish a learning review from a formal finding or discipline process.
Identify a process condition that contributed to a practice error.
Plan a proportionate improvement while preserving relevant responsibilities.
What is the better approach?
lessons.keyStatement: Examine how the work happened without promising that responsibility disappears.

items.title: Work path
items.body: Trace the relevant handoffs and checks. In the outdated-note case, ask who maintained the source and which version was verified before drafting. This examines a workplace practice that can be changed. It does not excuse the error or establish that a particular person was solely responsible.

items.title: Separate responsibilities
items.body: A learning discussion asks what the process can improve; an authorized formal process addresses matters within its role. Some issues need both. Do not promise immunity or use the group meeting to decide discipline. Coordinate the appropriate route while keeping the process-learning question clear.

items.title: Repair and review
items.body: Correct the material and assign a source-check responsibility with a review point. Check whether the next draft uses the verified source. A new checklist is implementation evidence, not proof that every error is prevented. The improvement should be specific enough to test and proportionate to the actual problem.

tabs.label: Public blame
tabs.body: Public blame can produce an immediate explanation but discourages disclosure and may conceal the handoff gap. It is not a substitute for relevant accountability. Examine the work path and use formal procedures where required rather than inviting the group to assign fault.

tabs.label: No accountability
tabs.body: A promise of no accountability can make disclosure easier briefly but exceeds the leader’s authority and weakens expectations. Learning works better when boundaries are honest. Examine conditions and coordinate formal matters without pretending responsibility cannot apply.

tabs.label: Learning with boundaries
tabs.body: Learning with boundaries corrects the work, examines conditions, and preserves proper authority. It gives the team an actionable improvement without deciding matters outside the discussion. Review its use and limits rather than declare that one repair solves all risk.

check.question: What is a useful response to the outdated eligibility note?
check.correct: Correct it, examine the source-check process, and coordinate any formal responsibility separately.
wrong: Publicly assign blame without reviewing the handoff.
Promise that no accountability can apply.
Declare a new checklist prevents every future error.
check.feedbackCorrect: The response separates correction, learning, and proper authority while making an improvement reviewable.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Public blame may miss the workplace practices, while immunity promises can exceed authority. A checklist also cannot prove that all error is gone. Correct the material, examine the process, and keep formal responsibilities in the appropriate route.

items.text: Which source and handoff led to the old note?
Who was responsible for verifying the source?
Assign a clear current-source check for the next draft.
Correct the inaccurate note through the proper process.
A group vote establishes discipline.
No mistake can ever require a formal response.

scenario.context: DHS practice case: After an outdated note reaches a draft, the leader wants the team either to blame one employee publicly or promise that no responsibility applies.
options: Choose whichever extreme makes the discussion shorter.
Separate correction, process learning, and any authorized formal responsibility.
Avoid the error because discussion might be uncomfortable.
responses: Neither shortcut examines the work appropriately.
This supports learning and relevant accountability together.
Avoidance leaves the problem and conditions unchanged.

lessons.transfer: Map a practice mistake to correction, process question, responsible route, and a measurable repair.

move.control: You can organize a bounded learning review and appropriate repair.
move.failure: Learning becomes either public blame or an unsupported immunity promise.

intro.heading: Recognize hierarchy and keep the right concern routes open
intro.body:
The leader who invites input may also control assignments, evaluations, and development. Staff can reasonably consider those consequences before disagreeing. An open-door statement is useful only when the response and available routes support it. Do not assume that silence from a newer employee means the employee has no concern.

In the practice form-review team, a temporary staff member sees an access problem but expects public disagreement with the project lead to harm future assignments. A prepared written route or an appropriate private conversation may make the contribution more usable. It should not require the person to explain personal history or speak on behalf of a whole group.

An ordinary design question can belong in the team’s decision process. An allegation of discrimination or another formal concern needs its proper route and duties. Do not keep it in the learning space or require the person to confront the supervisor first. The consultant can support thinking and capability, but should not become a permission gate for reporting.

lessons.keyStatement: An open-door statement is not enough when the leader controls opportunity.

items.title: Power
items.body: Consider who controls opportunity and whose contribution carries more risk. In the temporary-staff case, the leader may experience the question as routine while the staff member sees an assignment consequence. Recognizing that difference helps the leader design the route without claiming to know every person’s feelings.

items.title: Alternative
items.body: Offer a route that reaches the decision without forced public confrontation. A focused written question or an appropriate private contact can help. Confirm who reviews it and what influence remains possible. Do not offer a supposedly anonymous route unless its privacy and technical limits are actually established.

items.title: Formal concern
items.body: The substance of the concern determines whether a formal route is needed. If a report alleges protected-class harassment, the leader’s reporting responsibilities remain. A team-learning invitation cannot hold the allegation privately as a simulation or wait for consultant approval before the proper office is contacted.

tabs.label: Open door only
tabs.body: An open-door statement is easy to make but may still leave staff dependent on confronting the person who controls their work. Pair it with usable routes, accurate limits, and professional responses. Do not use lack of visitors as evidence that no concerns exist.

tabs.label: Usable route with limits
tabs.body: A usable route identifies the contact, timing, purpose, and information limits. It can give staff a practical alternative while preserving authority. Avoid an unverified anonymity promise and explain which concerns require another formal process.

tabs.label: Team-only rule
tabs.body: A team-only rule may be framed as keeping learning collaborative, but can block formal reporting access and necessary duties. Distinguish the design discussion from a complaint. Use the proper route without making the reporter complete a group conversation first.

check.question: How can the leader support a newer employee’s concern?
check.correct: Provide usable input routes and accurate boundaries while preserving formal reporting access.
wrong: Treat silence as proof of no concern.
Require public confrontation with the supervisor.
Promise anonymity without knowing the route’s limits.
check.feedbackCorrect: The response acknowledges power differences through practical access rather than unsupported guarantees.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Silence, forced confrontation, and an unverified anonymity promise can each hide a participation barrier. Explain usable routes and their limits, and keep formal reporting available without requiring a team-learning conversation first.

A junior employee expects social cost from public disagreement.
Written questions are reviewed before the decision closes.

lessons.statement: Review the response practice rather than score people’s willingness to speak.

image.caption: Colleagues share information and consider a decision together.

intro.heading: Review speaking-up practices without ranking employees
intro.body:
A leader can examine whether input routes and constructive responses were used. Were materials available before the meeting? Did a concern reach the decision? Was the answer or next step communicated? These are practical process questions. They do not by themselves produce a validated measure of psychological safety or establish how every employee feels.

In the practice team, an access concern raised through written input leads to a requirement check before the form is finalized. That shows a useful pathway from question to action. It does not prove that all staff now feel safe, that no one fears retaliation, or that every future question will be treated well.

Avoid ranking employees by how often they speak or creating a diagnostic label for a quiet team member. If surveys or broader climate work are used, follow appropriate privacy, design, and interpretation practices. A rise in reported concerns may reflect greater access, a new problem, or other conditions; the direction of the count alone cannot settle the explanation.

What should the review use?
lessons.keyStatement: Review the response practice rather than score people’s willingness to speak.

items.title: Process evidence
items.body: Trace one contribution from invitation to consideration and follow-through. In the form-review case, the written question reached a responsible requirement check before closure. This demonstrates the route’s use for that question. Check for missed inputs and explain the limits rather than report universal success.

items.title: Interpretation
items.body: Counts can have several explanations. More concerns may mean the route is more usable or that new problems occurred; fewer may mean improvement or silence. Pair the number with appropriate context and avoid a reassuring label when evidence is incomplete. Course completion is also activity rather than a climate result.

items.title: Privacy
items.body: Use appropriate information and do not score individual confidence from attendance, disclosure, or speaking turns. A quiet employee may contribute through written analysis. If a climate survey is planned, coordinate its design and small-group protections rather than attach personal rankings to a team-learning exercise.

tabs.label: Speaking count
tabs.body: A speaking count is easy to collect but can reward the visible format rather than meaningful contribution. It can overlook preparation, written input, or power differences. Review whether relevant knowledge entered the work instead of ranking people by airtime.

tabs.label: Process pathway
tabs.body: A process pathway shows what the team actually did with input. It supports a specific improvement question and can identify a missing follow-up. Its limit is that one working pathway does not establish everyone’s experience or a validated team score.

tabs.label: Safety declaration
tabs.body: A leader’s declaration may express intent, but cannot establish the shared expectation by itself. Review practices and appropriate evidence with limits. Do not use silence or a low report count as proof that the environment is safe for every person.

check.question: What can the written-input example establish?
check.correct: That one contribution reached an appropriate check before the decision, with broader conclusions still limited.
wrong: A lower complaint count always proves improvement.
check.feedbackCorrect: The evidence supports a bounded process result rather than an individual label or universal climate claim.
check.feedbackIncorrect: One successful pathway cannot establish every person’s experience. Quietness also does not measure courage, and counts alone have multiple explanations. Describe what happened to the input, what remains unknown, and the next practical review.

The leader explained the requirement-check result.
One example does not establish every staff member’s expectation.

Provide appropriate preparation and ways to contribute.

sections.heading: When people speak up
items: Acknowledge the contribution and examine its substance.
State knowledge limits and seek the evidence needed.
Use the proper formal route when a concern requires it.

sections.heading: Afterward
items: Explain what was considered and what happens next.
Assign a process improvement and review its use.
Protect personal information and avoid individual participation labels.

sources.title: Amy Edmondson — Psychological Safety and Learning Behavior in Work Teams
sources.note: Primary 1999 research introducing the team construct and examining its association with learning behavior in 51 manufacturing teams. It is not a guarantee of outcomes for DHS.

sources.title: AHRQ — Creating Psychological Safety in Teams
sources.note: Primary agency teaching resource on invitations, listening, knowledge limits, and responses. Healthcare practices inform general team learning here; this is not a clinical protocol.
